newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr plumbs 18-mth low on offshore rebuff.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr plumbs 18-mth low on offshore rebuff.

text.p: The Australian dollar plumbed fresh 18-month lows for the third session in a row Monday after overseas sellers buried a tentative rally.

Dealers said U.S. and Swiss banks mobbed the currency late Friday, wiping out all of the local day's hard won gains and more. The 1/2 cent setback was so swift and severe that many here had to bail out of long positions at a loss today, which saw it dip as deep as US$0.7378 and further soured sentiment.
Analysts thought the breach of US$0.7410 support bearish enough and looked for a decline to US$0.7350 near term, with a revisit of last year's 73 cent trough not far behind.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency was floundering at US$0.7375/80, its lowest close since January 25 last year, having sunk from an early US$0.7400/05 and US$0.7445/50 late here on Friday.
Dealers reported some exporter bids beneath US$0.7380 but doubted they would do more than delay the currency's descent given the weight advantage enjoyed by U.S. and Swiss sellers.
Chart watchers expected support levels at US$0.7370 and US$0.7350 to be mere pit stops on the road to US$0.7305.
Some reckoned the downtrend, which has already lasted four months and cost the dollar six cents, could stretch further.

"There are a lot of aligned reasons to suspect this is a modest target and the A$ has the capacity to extend losses to the 1995 low of US$0.7070," said Peter Pontikas, technical strategist at Westpac.
Chief amongst these was the disappearance of the currency's historic interest differential over the U.S. dollar.

After four Australian rate cuts totalling 200 basis points and with another already priced in by the market, parking your funds in the Australian dollar for three months earned you 5.14 percent while a deposit in the US$ made 5.66 percent. Similarly, the spread on 10-year bonds had narrowed to 17-year lows.

This was little less than revolutionary for offshore investors who had always thought of the A$ as a high yielding currency and was why many had abandoned it since the last official rate cut on May 23. The dollar had been up at 78 cents prior to this, meaning it had lost more than five percent since.
The market is tensed for an easing at any time, but analysts see good reason for the RBA to wait for consumer price and wages data next week to confirm the benign inflation outlook.
Indeed, a Reuter survey of economists forecasts Friday found a median of 1.7 percent for underlying inflation in the June quarter down from 2.1 percent in Q1.
That would be the lowest annual rate since the survey began in 1971 and support the argument that a loosening in official policy was needed just to keep real rates from rising.
The currency's fading yield attraction may not have been so telling had commodity prices had matched bullish expectations and resonded to signs of stronger, synchronised world growth.
Instead the price of many key commodities exported by Australia, including gold, copper, aluminium, wheat and oil, had been trending lower recently.
That was reflected in the closely followed Commodity Research Bureau index of futures prices.
The index hit two-year lows last week having lost around eight percent since late May.
And, with scant sign of inflation as yet in the U.S. or other major economies, analysts could see little reason why prices should recover anytime soon.

The dollar's weakness extended to most of the crosses, although a few like the German mark and Thai baht had even worse troubles of their own, and dragged the trade weighted index down to 56.5 from 56.9 late Friday and 59.0 before the last rate cut.
It was off at 83.70/80 yen from 84.67/77 but up at 1.3113/24 marks from 1.3059/70 late Friday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
